title: How do you ensure data quality in a pipeline (schema validation, null/range/uniqueness checks, reconciliation/row-count checks against source, data-contract tests, anomaly alerting), and what do you do when a pipeline fails in production (quarantine bad records to a DLQ, make steps idempotent so you can safely re-run, backfill, and alert with clear ownership)?
shortTitle: Ensuring data quality and handling pipeline failures in production

s1_definition.profdef: Data quality in a pipeline is the set of automated checks and contracts that guarantee data is correct, complete, and consistent as it flows from source to destination, including schema validation, null, range, and uniqueness checks, reconciliation and row-count checks against the source, data-contract tests between teams, and anomaly alerting. Handling a production failure means quarantining bad records to a dead-letter queue, making every step idempotent so you can safely re-run, backfilling any missed data, and alerting with clear ownership so someone accountable responds.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India's data pipeline as a quality line in a factory that produces financial reports. Data quality is the row of inspectors along the belt: one checks the form has the right shape (schema), one checks no mandatory box is blank and amounts are sensible (null and range), one checks no transaction id appears twice (uniqueness), one counts the output against what the source sent so nothing vanished (reconciliation), and one rings an alarm when today's numbers look wildly off (anomaly alerting). When something breaks, the factory does not panic: jammed forms go into a clearly labelled reject bin (dead-letter queue), every station is built so re-running a batch does not duplicate products (idempotency), missed batches are re-fed (backfill), and a named supervisor is paged to fix it (ownership).
s1_definition.oneliner: Enforce quality with schema, null, range, uniqueness, reconciliation, contracts, and anomaly checks; recover from failures with dead-letter queues, idempotent re-runs, backfills, and clear ownership.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Data quality in a pipeline is the set of automated checks and contracts that guarantee data is correct, complete, and consistent as it flows from source to destination, including schema validation, null, range, and uniqueness checks, reconciliation and row-count checks against the source, data-contract tests between teams, and anomaly alerting. Handling a production failure means quarantining bad records to a dead-letter queue, making every step idempotent so you can safely re-run, backfilling any missed data, and alerting with clear ownership so someone accountable responds.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India's data pipeline as a quality line in a factory that produces financial reports. Data quality is the row of inspectors along the belt: one checks the form has the right shape (schema), one checks no mandatory box is blank and amounts are sensible (null and range), one checks no transaction id appears twice (uniqueness), one counts the output against what the source sent so nothing vanished (reconciliation), and one rings an alarm when today's numbers look wildly off (anomaly alerting). When something breaks, the factory does not panic: jammed forms go into a clearly labelled reject bin (dead-letter queue), every station is built so re-running a batch does not duplicate products (idempotency), missed batches are re-fed (backfill), and a named supervisor is paged to fix it (ownership).

**One line to remember:** Enforce quality with schema, null, range, uniqueness, reconciliation, contracts, and anomaly checks; recover from failures with dead-letter queues, idempotent re-runs, backfills, and clear ownership.

sections.s2_technical:
Data quality begins with schema validation, confirming each record matches the expected structure and types, usually enforced by a schema registry with compatibility rules so a producer change cannot silently break the pipeline. Beyond structure you apply content checks: null checks ensure mandatory fields like account id and amount are present, range checks ensure values are sensible such as a non-negative amount within plausible bounds, and uniqueness checks ensure a key like transaction id is not duplicated. These are the day-to-day guards that catch the most common corruption.

Beyond per-record checks you verify the dataset as a whole. Reconciliation and row-count checks compare the pipeline's output against the source, so if the source sent a million rows and the warehouse has nine hundred thousand, you know data was lost and can halt or investigate rather than publish a wrong report. For money you also reconcile totals, confirming the sum of loaded amounts matches the source, which catches silent drops that row counts alone miss. Data-contract tests formalize the agreement between the producing team and the consuming team — the fields, types, semantics, and quality guarantees — and run as automated tests so a breaking change is caught in CI before it reaches production. Anomaly alerting watches metrics over time, like daily row counts or average amounts, and alerts when today deviates sharply from the norm, catching problems that pass structural checks but are still wrong.

When a pipeline fails in production, the first principle is isolation: quarantine bad records to a dead-letter queue so a single poison record does not block the whole flow, and keep the good data moving. The DLQ is owned and alerted so the quarantined records are investigated and reprocessed, not silently lost. The second principle is idempotency: every step is built so re-running it produces the same result, typically with upserts keyed by a stable id, so after a failure you can safely re-run without duplicating data. This is what makes recovery low-risk. The third is backfill: once the root cause is fixed, you reprocess the missed window by replaying from the durable log or re-reading the lake, and because the steps are idempotent the backfill corrects the data without double-counting. The fourth is alerting with clear ownership, so a failure pages a specific accountable team with context and a runbook, rather than a vague alert nobody acts on.

A senior nuance is where to place checks and how to fail. You validate early so bad data is caught at ingestion rather than after it has spread, you decide per check whether to fail the whole batch (for a critical reconciliation mismatch) or quarantine and continue (for a few bad records), and you make quality results observable with dashboards and a data catalog that records freshness and quality status. In a bank the stakes are high because the pipeline feeds balances, fraud decisions, and regulatory reports, so the bias is toward failing safe — halting or quarantining rather than publishing data you cannot vouch for — and toward full auditability so you can prove what was checked, what was quarantined, and how it was corrected.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Records may have nulls, bad amounts, or duplicate ids. This is exactly per-record quality checks plus a dead-letter queue.

Problem 2 — Data may silently go missing between source and target. This is exactly reconciliation and row-count checks.

Problem 3 — A failed run must be safely re-runnable and back-fillable. This is exactly idempotent upserts plus backfill.

The mini-project models a quality-gated pipeline. `QualityChecker` validates each record (schema, null, range, uniqueness), sending failures to a dead-letter queue. `Reconciler` compares loaded row count and total against the source and raises an alert on mismatch. `IdempotentTarget` upserts by id so re-runs and backfills do not duplicate. The demo runs a batch with bad records, reconciles, then backfills a previously missed record and re-runs to prove idempotency.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a source batch with two valid records (R1 1200, R2 5000), a duplicate R1, a null-amount R4, and an out-of-range R5, while R3 (1500) was missed this run. The source expects three valid rows totalling 7700.

Step 1 — Quality checks. The checker validates each record. R1 and R2 pass. The second R1 fails the uniqueness check, R4 fails the null check, and R5 fails the range check, so all three go to the dead-letter queue. Two good records remain.

Step 2 — Load good records. The two valid records are upserted into the idempotent target, which now holds R1 and R2 totalling 6200.

Step 3 — Reconcile. The reconciler compares the loaded two rows and 6200 total against the source expectation of three rows and 7700. They do not match, so it raises a mismatch, fails the batch, and alerts, because R3 was missed. This catches silent data loss that per-record checks alone would not.

Step 4 — Backfill and safe re-run. After investigation, the missed R3 (1500) is back-filled through the checks and upserted. The original good batch is also replayed to simulate a re-run, but because the target upserts by record id, R1 and R2 overwrite themselves instead of duplicating.

Step 5 — Reconcile again. The target now holds R1, R2, and R3, three rows totalling 7700, which matches the source expectation exactly. The pipeline quarantined bad records, detected the gap through reconciliation, and recovered safely through idempotent backfill with no duplication.

```
INFO: === Run 1: quality checks ===
WARNING: DLQ quarantine R1 reason=duplicate recordId
WARNING: DLQ quarantine R4 reason=null mandatory field
WARNING: DLQ quarantine R5 reason=amount out of range
INFO: UPSERT 2 records; target now has 2
INFO: DLQ size = 3
INFO: === Reconcile against source expectation (3 rows, 7700) ===
SEVERE: RECONCILE MISMATCH: source(rows=3,total=7700) vs loaded(rows=2,total=6200) → FAIL BATCH + ALERT
SEVERE: Batch failed reconciliation → investigate & backfill
INFO: === Backfill missed R3, then safe re-run (idempotent) ===
INFO: UPSERT 1 records; target now has 3
INFO: UPSERT 2 records; target now has 3
INFO: === Reconcile after backfill ===
INFO: RECONCILE OK: rows=3 total=7700
```


sections.s6_takeaway:
I ensure data quality with layered automated checks. It begins with schema validation, confirming each record matches the expected structure and types, usually enforced by a schema registry with compatibility rules. Then come content checks: null checks for mandatory fields like account id and amount, range checks so values are sensible like a non-negative amount within plausible bounds, and uniqueness checks so a key like transaction id is never duplicated. Beyond per-record checks I verify the dataset as a whole with reconciliation and row-count checks against the source, and for money I also reconcile total sums, so if the source sent a million rows or a given total and the target does not match, I know data was lost and can halt rather than publish a wrong report. I add data-contract tests that formalize the agreement between producing and consuming teams and run in CI so a breaking change is caught before production, and anomaly alerting that watches metrics over time and flags when today's row counts or averages deviate sharply from the norm.

When a pipeline fails in production I follow four principles. First, isolation: I quarantine bad records to a dead-letter queue so one poison record never blocks the flow, and the DLQ is owned and alerted so those records are investigated, not lost. Second, idempotency: every step uses upserts keyed by a stable id so I can safely re-run after a failure without duplicating data. Third, backfill: once the root cause is fixed I reprocess the missed window by replaying from the durable log or re-reading the lake, and because the steps are idempotent the backfill corrects the data without double-counting. Fourth, alerting with clear ownership so a failure pages a specific accountable team with context and a runbook. A senior point I add is to validate early so bad data is caught at ingestion, to decide per check whether to fail the whole batch or quarantine and continue, and to make quality observable through dashboards and a catalog.

In my project at the National Bank of India this is exactly how the pipeline behaved. Quality checks quarantined duplicate, null, and out-of-range records to a dead-letter queue, and a reconciliation step caught a run where a record had been missed by comparing row counts and totals against the source, failing the batch and alerting the on-call team rather than publishing an incomplete report. We then back-filled the missing record and safely re-ran, and because every write was an idempotent upsert, the re-run corrected the data without duplicating anything, after which reconciliation passed. Because this pipeline fed balances, fraud decisions, and regulatory reports, the bias was always to fail safe and keep full auditability, so we could prove what was checked, what was quarantined, and how it was corrected.
